Several F10 signals together: a landmark claim with no engagement in ~4 months; a patch history in which each of two prior versions was conceded erroneous and the threshold changed every time; later work on the same question (Ge et al., July 2026; Axante et al., Sept 2026) treats the conjecture as open without citing it; erdosproblems.com still lists it open.

The proof is developed by GPT6 under the authors' guidance, and is human-checked by the authors.

why: The only claims of the whole statement are Fukuyama's three versions and Mitchell's Zenodo proof. v1 and v2 are knocked down by the author's own admission of errors, and Mitchell's proof was retracted. Fukuyama v3 is the close call. Silence alone would only make it unreviewed. I set it aside as not credible because several signals appear together: two conceded errors in a row, a threshold that changed with each version, no reaction for four months to a claim that would be a landmark, and later papers on this exact conjecture (Ge et al., Axante et al.) that still treat it as open without citing v3. Balogh et al., Ge et al. and Mishra each prove the conjecture's shape only for a restricted class (VC-dimension 1, bounded VC-dimension, shifted families), so each is a case. Fukuyama's sub-logarithmic base and Axante's lower bound on the growth base move quantities but leave the question open, so both are bounds. Duke–Erdős, vector-space, subsets-of-[n], Talagrand and Γ-condition work are variants. Small f(n,3) values are instances. The model credit for the Mitchell proof is only a co-creator listing that says nothing about what the model did, so it is none. Fang–Wang's GPT6 proof is generated, but its event is a variant.
doubts: Fukuyama v3 being not_credible is a judgement call. Fukuyama is an established author, and the record never says whether Ge et al. or Axante et al. explicitly call the problem open. They only state the conjecture and prove it in restricted settings. If a reader judges those signals too weak, v3 would be credible-but-doubtful and the whole-statement claim would count. Balogh et al. reach the conjectured shape only at d=1. For bounded d>1 a log* factor remains, so labelling that event a case leans on the d=1 class. In Mishra's paper, 'shifted families' is undefined in the text that was read.
